title: Meeting Rooms
statement:
You're given a list of `intervals`, where `intervals[i] = [start, end]` is one meeting that begins at `start` and ends at `end`. Return `True` if a single person could attend every meeting, and `False` if any two meetings overlap.

A meeting that ends at the exact moment another one starts does not overlap it. The meetings may be given in any order, and the list may be empty.

Constraints: 0 to 5,000 meetings; 0 <= start < end <= 1,000,000.

examples.explanation: Sorted by start the meetings are [1, 4], [5, 8], [9, 12], and none overlap.
The second meeting starts at 5, before the first one ends at 6.
One meeting ends at 3 exactly when the next starts, which is allowed.

hints: If two meetings overlap, is there some ordering of the list in which you could always spot a clash by looking only at neighbours?
Checking every pair works but is slow for thousands of meetings. What ordering lets you check each meeting against just one other?
After arranging the meetings by start time, which single earlier meeting could clash with the current one?
What does it mean for a meeting to clash with the one before it? Compare the previous end with the current start, and decide whether equal counts as a clash.
Sort by start time and compare each consecutive pair: if the earlier meeting's end is greater than the later meeting's start, return False; otherwise return True at the end.
followUps: What are the time and space complexity, and what dominates?
Why does sorting by start time mean you only have to compare neighbours?
What would change if a meeting ending exactly when another begins should count as a clash?
How would you report which two meetings clash instead of only True or False?
idealAnswerPoints: Sorts the meetings by start time
Compares each meeting only with the one before it
Uses prev_end <= next_start so back-to-back meetings are allowed
Handles an empty list or a single meeting, and states O(n log n) time
weakAnswerSigns: Compares every pair of meetings, O(n^2), without noting it
Compares neighbours without sorting first and misses clashes between unsorted entries
Uses < so back-to-back meetings are rejected
Sorts by end time but compares the wrong fields

rubric.correctness: Correct for unsorted input, back-to-back meetings, nested and identical meetings, and empty or single-meeting lists.
rubric.efficiency: O(n log n) from the sort plus a linear scan; the all-pairs check is acceptable only if named as O(n^2).
rubric.code_quality: Sort plus a single neighbour check, no unnecessary nested loops or flags.
rubric.communication: Explains why sorting makes neighbour checks sufficient and states how equal times are treated.
